idea.idea: Checklist: Why your AI projects fail due to fragmented data
idea.angle: Fix your scattered data across WhatsApp and notebooks before spending money on 'AI'
idea.audience_problem: Owners buy AI tools but fail to get results because their source data is unorganized.

hooks: Why your AI tools fail on scattered business data
Stop buying AI subscriptions before fixing messy shop ledgers
Why AI models crash without clean customer history
piece.hook_reason: It directly targets Indian SMB owners who buy AI software expecting miracles, pointing right to the root cause: fragmented internal business data across WhatsApp and paper ledgers.

slides.title: Why your AI tools fail on scattered business data
slides.subtitle: Clean up your notebooks, WhatsApp chats, and item rates before buying subscriptions.

slides.myth: Buying a smarter AI model fixes messy business reporting.
slides.fact: AI models are like electricity. Value comes from clean customer history, item rates, and logged decisions you feed them.

slides.title: Check these 4 items before buying AI
items: Standardized item names across stock ledgers and bill books
Clear history of customer discounts and credit terms
Written rules on who can approve custom rates
Organized digital folder of past invoices and receipts

slides.title: 4 steps to ready your data for AI
items: Audit where customer chats and quote history live
Unify stock names across paper registers and sheets
Write explicit guardrails for custom rates or credit
Test prototype setups on edge cases before launch

slides.title: 4 rules for AI that actually works
items: Treat AI like a new junior staff member
Set guardrails and audit decisions before delegating
Keep historical data secure with strict access permissions
Fix workflow bottlenecks before paying for software

piece.caption: Fixing fragmented business data across WhatsApp chats and paper registers before implementing AI automation. Say you run an electrical supply shop in Pune with three billing counters. If your item rates, customer credit terms, and GST numbers are scattered across WhatsApp chats and paper notebooks, no AI tool can generate accurate quotes or payment reminders. AI models act like electricity; what matters is the business context you plug into them. Start by standardizing your inventory unit names and margin rules across your team. Build quick prototypes to test edge cases before paying annual software fees. Pine Labs cut support tickets by nearly 40% with their assistant Guide by treating AI like a new employee—training it, setting strict permissions, and auditing decisions. Where is your shop customer data currently stored?

Access to powerful AI is no longer the hard part. As frontier and open-source models get cheaper and more interchangeable, the real question for businesses is what they own that others cannot copy.
That question anchored the TechSparks 2026 session ‘ Beyond the model: The moat for durable AI .’ Divakaran Ullampuzha Mana, Director of Solutions Architecture, India, MongoDB; Vijeth Pandit, CPO, Pine Labs Payments; and Karan Kumar, VP, Product, Spinny, spoke with Shivani Muthanna, Senior Director, Strategic Content & Video, YourStory, about what companies must own to build AI that lasts.
Models are electricity, context is the moat
Mana began by noting that open-source models are catching up with frontier models in capability and performance, and access costs keep falling. What separates one business from another, he said, is how seamlessly it can access its own enterprise data, which sits across systems in structured and unstructured formats, and turn it into insight or action.
Pandit pointed to distribution and accumulated experience. Pine Labs works with almost three million merchants and hundreds of banks in India and globally. He noted that “models in isolation will only help in inferring”, and that the interactions, data, and history a company builds are what make a product relevant.
Kumar offered an analogy. “I look at models as electricity,” he said, adding that the winner is decided by what a company plugs in and what the layers on top are built to solve. At Spinny, those layers rest on verified definitions of internal metrics, the reasoning behind past decisions, and how the team runs and evaluates experiments. Connected through their internal operating system AIR, this becomes context that competitors cannot easily replicate.
Building a demo is easy, Mana said, because “you can actually build a beautiful agentic system that looks like magic”. The trouble starts when thousands of concurrent users and vast stores of documents need to be accessed and used by AI applications/agents, under strict security and compliance rules. Companies that succeed begin with a governed, secure data foundation, then add evaluation frameworks, observability, memory systems, and runtime engines. Those that do, he said, convert pilots to production at a high rate and ship the next use case faster.
Pandit said Pine Labs treats agents much like human employees: train them, set guardrails, audit their judgment, and delegate more as confidence grows. The company built the Grantex protocol to define what an agent can and cannot do, and P3P, a protocol that lets buyer and seller agents transact. In one example, a shopper sets a mandate for a festive flash sale, and the agent buys only when the price falls below the threshold.
Mana said security has to be built from the ground up. That means encryption at rest, in transit, and during queries, least-privilege access, and agents that inherit the permissions of the person running them rather than using service accounts. Every step an agent takes should also be traceable and replayable.
Kumar said Spinny starts from consumer problems rather than solutions, with car discovery as the big one. Its conversational navigation lets buyers describe what they want in their own words, and AI also supports inspection and pricing. Voice AI has proven its return first, with vision AI still on the path. “How we look at it is what is the cost of not doing it, rather than the cost of doing it,” he said.
Pandit said Pine Labs product managers now build prototypes instead of writing PRDs, which surfaces edge cases earlier. The company manages more products with the same headcount, and its merchant assistant, Guide, has cut support tickets by almost 40%.
Closing the session, Mana listed three priorities: a sound data strategy, workflows redesigned to learn from their outcomes rather than mimic old ones, and security and governance in place from the start so AI behavior stays predictable.
If the model is something every company can access, then durability has to come from what sits around it. As the conversation made clear, that means proprietary data and context, memory that agents can rely on, workflows that improve with use, and the trust and control that let businesses put AI to work on real decisions.
